searches.note: Twenty two searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's; six were left unspent. Ten were restricted to an own domain and read as primary through their summaries: the regulating council's doriasbaixas.com twice (the history of 1980 and 1988, the subzone rules), pazodesenorans.com once, fefinanes.com four times, martincodax.com twice and terrasgauda.com once; one more to the importer's demaisonselections.com. The rest went to the open web for the second source of each date and person (the pazo and its distillery, the palace of Fefiñanes and its viscount, the founding of Fefiñanes, the founding of Martín Códax, the Vindel parchment, Do Ferreiro's founding and making, Terras Gauda's making and founding) and one to whether a founder of Pazo de Señorans has died. The two shared searches, the council's history and its subzone rules, serve all five. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages for their own dates, vineyards and methods and to the regulating council for the law, then to the open web for the second source of each date and person.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail rested on one account, or the accounts disagreed, it was said with less (the father's trade, the eleven months, the year the winery took the poet's name).

Sources whose address carries a living person's name (the Spanish Wine Lover, Wine Scholar Guild and Wines of Galicia pages on Do Ferreiro, all three under the founder's company name) and a writer's own site (on Pazo de Señorans and Terras Gauda) were met in the results but are never cited, here or in the fragment; where one of them is the second source of a fact, the review names its publisher only.

The fragment's own sources were kept as the author wrote them but for two: Terras Gauda's Bodeboca sheet gave way to the house's own tasting notes, and Do Ferreiro's Wine.com sheet to the regulating council's history; the new ones are listed per record under extraSources.

tested: Founded 1989: the library's year; a Spanish merchant gives the first harvest as 1989 and another account the first labelled wine as the 1990 vintage. The story says the family began making wine there in 1989; confirmed.

The pazo of the sixteenth century at Vilanoviña, Meis: the house's visit sheet, El Español and most listings; one listing says the fourteenth century. Confirmed as the house's date, which the story hedges.
The distillery for orujo: Vinissimus and a Galician shop list the house's own orujo, double distilled in copper; confirmed.

The making: the house's own shop sheets give stainless steel, more than thirty months on the lees in tank, no malolactic, fermentation at 16 degrees and a five year window; confirmed. The year in bottle before release rests on European Cellars and the Wine Scholar Guild guide, not on the house; it stands as theirs.
The site: the house's shop sheet names the plot Os Bancales, with vines of more than forty five years; European Cellars puts it on the slope behind the estate. Confirmed, and the name added.

The Denominación: the regulating council gives 11 October 1980 for the Denominación Específica Albariño, its rules of 1984, the ratification of July 1988 (28 July by one of its pages; a provisional order of March and the rules of 4 July by another), the three first subzones and the reason the grape's name could not stand; confirmed.
The serve, 10 to 12 degrees Celsius in a wide glass, agrees with the Codex's full whites. The questions: one key each, four makings and four years, explanations that teach; sound.
The rules: nobody living named (the founding couple described), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no ranking word; British; no dash. Sound.

tested: 1928: the house's pages and its technical sheet give the brand and label created and registered in 1928, the label drawn by a Santiago jeweller, jet carver and designer, and the first harvest of the wine in 1928; a merchant's account gives the first vintage released that year; confirmed.
1929: the house gives an award at the Barcelona international fair of 1929 and 1930; confirmed as the house's, which the story hedges.

1583 and the first viscount: the house's 1583 page says that in 1583 was born, at Fefiñanes, the man who would be the first viscount, in the service of his country and his king, who carried on his forebears' work and finished the palace; the town's page dates the building's start to the sixteenth century under a lord of Fefiñanes, and a second account gives its completion in the seventeenth by his nephew, the first viscount, a title granted by Philip IV. Confirmed; the story's telling agrees with both.
The making and serve: the house's 2023 sheet gives fermentation in stainless steel at a low temperature, bottling in the first half of the following year and a serve of 10 degrees Celsius; confirmed.

The others: the house gives 1995 as the first vintage of 1583, fermented in Bordeaux barrels of one to five years' use (French barriques on its English sheet), a short time on the lees, then steel; and III Año fermented in steel and held long on its lees and in tank; confirmed.
founded: 1904, with the bodega's two founders, is given by Kysela and by Vinissimus, but the house says only the first years of the twentieth century; the author's empty field stands.
One of the first white wines of the region with a commercial label: Wine Traveler and a tourism listing say the first bottled Albariño, in 1928; the record's softer claim stands.
The questions: one key each, four makings and four years; sound. The rules: nobody living named, the jeweller and the viscount described, no price, no score, no ranking word; British; no dash. Sound.
open: founded stays empty: 1904 has two secondary sources (Kysela, Vinissimus) but no primary; the integrator may set it if the house's own year is found.
The jeweller who drew the label is named by the house; his dates were not found, so he stays described.

tested: Founded 1985 by fifty growers: the house's winery page says so, and Escoladist and a trade directory give 1985 independently; confirmed. The plan's and the region record's 1986 is the year of the first Martín Códax Albariño, on the house's wines page.

Cooperative: a directory account gives the first body as an association of Albariño growers of Vilariño and Cambados that became a company and took the name Bodegas Martín Códax in 1998, and two accounts speak of a cooperative; the record's growers' winery stands, and the story no longer says the winery took the poet's name in 1985.

The poet and the parchment: IMSLP, the Cervantes library and OMI give seven cantigas de amigo, music over six of them with the sixth staff empty, the parchment of the late thirteenth century found by the Madrid antiquarian bookseller Pedro Vindel in 1913 or 1914, used as a book cover, and held by the Morgan Library as MS M.979; confirmed, and the label line corrected to six with their music.

The making: the house's pages give hand picking into small cases, plots in the heart of the Salnés and time on the lees; confirmed. The house's Lías sheet gives six to seven months on the lees with stirring and up to twelve months more in tank; the note is corrected.
Vindel: the house names the wine for the manuscript of the poet's songs; confirmed.
The Val do Salnés rule in the trap (at least seven tenths Albariño) and the varietal rule in the wine question: the regulating council's wines page; confirmed.

The serve, 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, and the window are a young white's; sound. The questions: four blends and four places, one key each; sound. The rules: nobody living named, the membership counts left out as volatile; British; no dash. Sound.

tested: Founded 1973: De Maison gives a first wine without labels in 1973 and the first labelled release about a decade later; Spanish Wine Lover and the Wine Scholar Guild guide (both under the founder's company name, so not cited) give 1973 as the start of the business and a first harvest with his father. Confirmed.

The name: De Maison says the wine was named in homage to the family's blacksmith trade, and Spanish Wine Lover that the founder came from a family of blacksmiths; neither says the father. Changed to the family's old trade.

The founding of the Denominación: the regulating council counts fourteen promoters, and fourteen wineries on its register in 1988; a Spanish guide puts the founder among the first fourteen; no source read names the son. Changed to the founder alone, with the council's count.

The plot: De Maison and a guide put the historic plot in front of the family house at Lores; its age is given as planted in 1785, documented in 1850, more than two hundred years and more than two hundred and fifty, pre phylloxera; Bodeboca gives the pergola. The record's more than two hundred years and the eighteenth century stand.

The making: native yeasts (De Maison, Spanish Wine Lover, Vinissimus), stainless steel (Bodeboca, Spanish Wine Lover); the lees time is eleven months for the 2024 (De Maison), about twelve (Gourmet Hunters) and a little over a year for the 2007 (Directo al Paladar). Changed to about a year.

The ageing of ten to twenty years is the importer's and is hedged as such; the serve agrees with the Codex's full whites. The questions: four trainings and four meanings, one key each; the story explanation changed with the story. The rules: the founder, his son and daughter never named; no price, no score; British; no dash. Sound after the changes.

tested: The grapes: the house's 2023 sheet gives seventy per cent Albariño, twenty five Caíño and five Loureiro; merchants give seventy, twenty and ten in other years. The record's about seven tenths, with shares changing by year, stands.

The making: the house's sheet gives a cold soak before fermentation whose length differs by variety, fermentation with its own yeasts from its own vineyards (a pied de cuve, no foreign yeast) and stabilising before bottling; Vinissimus's page on the house gives each variety vinified apart and wild yeasts; Enterwine and Vinissimus give stainless steel. Confirmed.

The O Rosal rule: the regulating council's wines page and its rules of 2009 give at least seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira for Rías Baixas Rosal, with every grape from the subzone; Condado do Tea pairs Albariño with Treixadura; the three first subzones of 1988. The record's wording set the subzone on the seventy per cent only; corrected in four places.
Founded: 1989 in several accounts, with a first vintage in 1990 (Rías Baixas Wines, Enterwine), and 1990 in a brand profile; the empty field and the story's turn of the 1990s stand.

Caíño Blanco: the grape had nearly vanished by the 1980s and the house set out to replant it (Rías Baixas Wines, Cellar Tours, Interempresas, the importer); another producer elsewhere is also credited with reviving it, so the record's set out to restore, never alone, stands.

Etiqueta Negra: the house's 2016 sheet gives the musts fermented in French oak barrels, then lees ageing; a merchant's 2021 sheet gives each variety in French oak foudres and barrels. The note is said with less.

The serve, 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, and the window are a young white's; sound. The questions: four makings and four grapes, one key each, explanations that teach; sound. The rules: the founding family described, its two children never named, the share of the region's Caíño Blanco left out as volatile; British; no dash. Sound.
